opus-5.5.text:
I think algorithm research becomes more important, not less, though its role shifts a bit.

For the past several years the dominant story has been scaling: take the Transformer, add more data and more compute, and things keep getting better. In that regime, architecture work could feel secondary. Many clever ideas gave a small gain at small scale and then vanished once you scaled up, because scale washed them out. So people became skeptical, and somewhat reasonably.

But once you start hitting the data wall, where high-quality human text is running out, and the compute wall, where each additional order of magnitude gets very expensive, the question changes. It's no longer "how do we get more resources?" It's "how do we get more out of the resources we already have?" That is exactly an algorithmic question. How much intelligence can you extract per token of data and per FLOP of compute? Efficiency stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the main lever.

From my own corner, sequence modeling and efficient attention, I see this very concretely. Standard softmax attention has quadratic cost in sequence length, and at inference the KV cache keeps growing. That was tolerable when contexts were a few thousand tokens. Now we want models that reason for very long chains of thought, work as agents over long horizons, and read entire codebases or long documents. Test-time compute is becoming a major axis of scaling, and if inference is your bottleneck, then the architecture's inference efficiency matters enormously. That's why linear attention, state space models, and things like DeltaNet and gated variants have come back into focus. They're not just academic curiosities anymore. They address a real systems constraint.

I'd also emphasize that good algorithm research now has to be hardware-aware. An idea that looks elegant on paper but can't use tensor cores efficiently, or can't be parallelized during training, won't survive. A lot of my work has gone into making these recurrent-style models trainable at scale, for example with chunkwise parallel forms, so they can actually compete with Transformers on wall-clock time, not just in theoretical complexity. I think the algorithm and the kernel increasingly need to be designed together.

Then there's data efficiency, which is the deeper and harder question. If data is limited, we need architectures and training objectives with better inductive biases, ones that generalize more from less, handle state tracking and length extrapolation better, and do more genuine computation per token. Some of the expressivity results, like what kinds of state tracking different recurrent models can or can't do, matter here because they tell us where the current architectures are fundamentally limited.

So my view is that the "bitter lesson" doesn't really say algorithms don't matter. It says methods that scale with compute win. As compute and data get constrained, the methods that make better use of compute are the ones that scale. That's a big opportunity for algorithm researchers, and especially for people who can bridge theory, architecture, and systems.

r001.rationale: It says scaling data and compute made architecture work seem secondary, but does not explain that abundant, scalable data reduced the incentive to research data efficiency.

r002.rationale: It argues that data and compute limits shift the focus to extracting more from existing resources, making algorithmic efficiency a central lever.

r003.rationale: It presents data and compute as constrained resources and algorithms as necessary to use them efficiently, including through data-efficient architectures and training.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd push back a little on the framing that we're "running into" limits, because I think the limits were always there — we just weren't close enough to feel them. For a long time, the easiest way to get a better model was to add more data and more GPUs, and the Transformer with full attention was good enough that nobody needed to ask whether it was the right architecture. Scaling was the algorithm.

Now the cheap wins are mostly spent. High-quality text on the internet is finite. Compute keeps growing, but the cost of training a frontier model has gone from "a lab budget" to "a national budget," and inference cost is becoming the thing that actually constrains what you can deploy. So the question shifts from "how much can we afford to throw at this" to "how much do we get back per unit of what we throw."

That's where algorithm research comes back in, and I think it comes back in two ways.

The first is efficiency, which is where my own work sits. Full attention is quadratic in sequence length and the KV cache grows linearly, so if you want long context, many agents, long reasoning chains, the architecture itself becomes the bottleneck. Linear attention, state-space models, delta-rule style recurrent models — the point of all of that is to make the model's cost scale with the useful information, not with raw length. For a while people treated these as toy alternatives. Now that the Transformer is actually hitting the wall at inference time, they're getting a real second look, and hybrids are showing up in production models.

The second is sample efficiency, which I think is the bigger long-term story. Humans don't need a trillion tokens to learn language. If the data is capped, the only way forward is to learn more from each token — better objectives, better use of synthetic data and RL, architectures with better inductive biases. That's not a solved problem at all, and it's fundamentally an algorithm question, not an infrastructure question.

So I'd say the role of algorithm research is moving from a supporting role back to a driving role. The last few years taught us that scale matters enormously. The next few will be about figuring out what to scale, and how to not waste it.

r001.rationale: It says that adding more data and GPUs was the easiest route to better models, so researchers did not need to ask whether the architecture was right. This conveys that scaling data reduced the incentive to pursue data efficiency.

r002.rationale: It describes finite high-quality data and rising compute costs, then says algorithm research is returning to a driving role through efficiency and sample efficiency.

r003.rationale: The response discusses data and compute as constraints and algorithms as a way to improve efficiency, but does not clearly present all three as jointly indispensable to AI development.

astra-6.text:
I think algorithm research becomes more important as we run into those limits, but the question we ask changes. Instead of asking only, “Can we get better performance if we make the model bigger?” we ask, “How much learning can we get from a fixed amount of data and computation?”

There are several ways to approach that. We can improve how models learn from each example, build architectures that spend less computation on redundant work, and make inference more adaptive. An easy question shouldn’t necessarily require the same amount of computation as a difficult one.

And these limits are connected. If you try to address a shortage of data by generating synthetic data, you spend compute, and you still need a way to distinguish useful information from repeated mistakes. So the algorithmic problem isn’t simply producing more tokens. It’s creating a learning process that makes reliable progress.

I’d also distinguish an improvement on a benchmark from an improvement in efficiency. If a method performs better but requires much more tuning or data preparation, those costs matter. The meaningful comparison is what you can achieve with the same total budget.

So I see the role shifting toward making scaling more productive: understanding what computation is actually doing, where it’s wasted, and how to get more capability out of the resources we have.

r001.rationale: The response describes how algorithm research matters under data and compute limits, but does not say that the ability to scale data previously reduced the incentive to research data efficiency.

r002.rationale: It says algorithm research becomes more important as data and compute limits arise and describes ways algorithms can improve learning and efficiency.

r003.rationale: It connects data, computation, and algorithms: the response discusses learning within fixed data and compute budgets, how synthetic data consumes compute, and how algorithms can make learning more productive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think algorithm research becomes more important when we can no longer assume that more data and more compute will solve the next problem. The question shifts from “How large can we make the model?” to “How much can we learn with the resources we have?”

That opens up several directions: learning more efficiently from limited data, using computation more selectively, and designing models with better assumptions about the structure of a problem. We also need to understand why a method works, because an improvement that holds at one scale may disappear at another.

But I wouldn’t draw a sharp line between algorithms and scaling. A better algorithm can make a previously unaffordable scale practical. So the role of research is partly to find new capabilities, and partly to reduce the cost of reaching them. Under resource constraints, that second role becomes especially valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says data efficiency matters under limits, but does not explain that the ability to keep scaling data had reduced the incentive to research it.

r002.rationale: It says algorithm research becomes more important when data and compute can no longer simply be increased to solve the next problem.

r003.rationale: It discusses data, algorithms, and compute, but does not clearly state that all three are jointly indispensable to AI development.
